The upcoming MacBook Ultra was never going to be cheap, and beyond the all-new thinner design, OLED display, and touch functionality, there's also the added cost of rising memory prices to consider. The latest reports suggest its production costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has traditionally preferred to arrange multiple suppliers for components to ensure a stable display supply and secure the best pricing, and the company originally hoped to adopt the same strategy for the MacBook Ultra. However, according to supply chain sources, Apple has decided to use only a single display supplier...

Apple has three display partners across its product lineup: Samsung, LG, and BOE. BOE currently only supplies screens for Apple's lower-tier products, while the higher-end display orders are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever on an Apple product. Combining two-stack tandem OLED with touch functionality, and applying it to the larger sizes required for a laptop, is no small feat. The latest supply chain reports indicate that Apple has decided to exclusively source these screens from Samsung.

The Elec reports that LG failed to meet Apple's desired production volume requirements.

Apple required large-scale mass production using large substrates. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6th-generation OLED production line, while LG Display is reportedly considering continuing to use its existing 6th-generation production line. Although OLED panels for laptops can be produced using a 6th-generation line, both substrate efficiency and production capacity are lower than those of the 8.6th-generation line. Because initial product volumes were too low, Apple chose Samsung Display as its exclusive supplier.

Since LG's production capacity is limited, the added logistical complexity of a dual-supplier arrangement simply wasn't worthwhile. As expected, LG is unlikely to have the opportunity to produce screens for this flagship MacBook until at least 2029.

This clearly puts Samsung in a stronger position in panel price negotiations, which is expected to drive up Apple's production costs. As always, Apple will most likely pass these costs on to consumers, much as it has done with rising memory costs.

Given that the MacBook Ultra's price could be staggeringly high, how interested are you in considering an upgrade? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
